title: Test Reporting
concept:
**Test reporting** communicates test progress, product quality, and risks to stakeholders so they can make informed decisions. Two kinds of report are typical.

**Test progress report** (interim) — issued periodically during testing. Audience: project manager, product owner, sponsors. Contents:
- Test execution status (planned / executed / passed / failed / blocked).
- Defects found / fixed / open by severity.
- Coverage achieved against plan.
- Risks (new, changed, retired).
- Issues blocking progress.
- Forecast: when will exit criteria be met?

**Test summary report** (final) — issued at the end of a test level or release. Audience: same plus broader stakeholders. Contents:
- Final test execution numbers.
- Final defect status (open defects, accepted residual risk).
- Coverage achieved.
- Exit criteria status (met / waived).
- Lessons learned.
- Recommendations for next release.

Good reports are **actionable** (each finding leads to a decision), **audience-tailored** (an executive cares about residual risk; a developer cares about open defects), **honest** (bad news travels first), and **visualised** (charts beat tables for trends).

In Agile, much of this reporting is replaced by live dashboards, but a written summary at release time is still common.
keyPoints: Two main reports: progress (interim) and summary (final).
Contents: execution status, defects, coverage, risks, exit criteria.
Reports must be actionable, audience-tailored, honest, and visualised.

quiz.question: Which item is MOST likely to appear in a final test summary report but NOT in an interim progress report?
options: Lessons learned and recommendations for the next release.
quiz.explanation: Lessons learned and recommendations for next release are retrospective — they belong in the final summary report after testing completes. Execution status, open defects, and current coverage are progress-report content and continue to appear in the summary.
